subject: English
q: What is the function of the semicolon in: “Some candidates prefer English literature; others choose history.”?
o: It joins two closely related independent clauses
explanation: The semicolon links two complete clauses that balance each other without a conjunction.

subject: English
q: The sentence “The exams are over, the students have gone home.” contains a comma splice. Which punctuation mark should replace the comma?
explanation: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses; a comma alone cannot.

subject: English
q: Identify the sentence with correct punctuation usage.
o: The owner, sells tea at reasonable prices.
The shops tea is famous across the city.
The market sells two kinds of rice; basmati and brown.
The shop sells three kinds of tea: green, black and herbal.
explanation: A colon after a complete clause correctly introduces the list; the others misuse a semicolon before a list, omit a possessive apostrophe, or put a comma between subject and verb.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
o: The team includes: Ali, Sara and Bilal.
She brought everything we needed: maps, torches and water.
We will meet at: the library after lunch.
He is: the best player in the squad.
explanation: A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it cannot come between a verb or preposition and its object or complement.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
o: I wanted to go to the lecture; however, I had a fever.
Because it was raining; the match was postponed.
He bought; apples, bananas and grapes.
The minister arrived; and the ceremony began.
explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, often before “however”; it cannot follow a dependent clause, introduce a list, or stand before “and” in a simple compound sentence.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
o: The girls’ hostel is near the main gate.
The hostel has it’s own mess.
The student’s were given new books.
explanation: “Girls’ hostel” correctly marks the possessive of a plural; “it’s” means “it is”, plurals take no apostrophe, and “hers” never has one.

subject: English
q: In which sentence is the comma used correctly?
o: The bus broke down, we walked home.
The guests, arrived late for dinner.
The clerk handed, the file to the officer.
After the meeting ended, the members had lunch.
explanation: A comma after an introductory clause is correct; the others separate a subject from its verb, create a comma splice, or split a verb from its object.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses quotation marks correctly?
o: “Keep your phones outside said the supervisor.”
“We will begin at nine,” said the invigilator.
The principal said “that the school would close early.”
“The hall is full” announced the guard.
explanation: Only the first places the comma inside the closing quotation mark and encloses just the spoken words; reported speech with “that” takes no quotation marks.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses a hyphen correctly?
o: The company hired a highly-qualified accountant.
The company hired a full-time accountant.
The company hired an accountant who is newly-appointed.
explanation: A compound adjective before a noun (“full-time accountant”) is hyphenated; compounds with an -ly adverb are not, and the hyphen in “works-full” is meaningless.

subject: English
q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
o: How many tickets did you buy, for the match?
Where did you park the car?
explanation: A direct question ends with a question mark and needs no internal comma here; the others end a question with a full stop or insert needless commas.

subject: English
q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
o: Bilal have you finished, the report?
Sara, have you seen my notes?
explanation: The name of the person addressed is followed by a comma, and a direct question ends with a question mark.

subject: English
q: Which of the following sentences contains a comma splice?
o: The shop was closed, we went home.
Because the lights failed, the play stopped.
The road was blocked, so the bus turned back.
The rain fell; the streets flooded.
explanation: The first sentence joins two independent clauses with only a comma; the others use a conjunction, subordination or a semicolon.

subject: English
q: Which sentence punctuates the direct speech correctly?
o: He said, “I have finished the report.”
explanation: A comma follows the reporting verb, the quotation begins with a capital, and the final full stop goes inside the closing quotation mark.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses “however” with correct punctuation?
o: The staff were trained however, mistakes continued.
The shop was busy; however it, made little profit.
The road was repaired, however it flooded again.
The plan was sound; however, it was never implemented.
explanation: Between two independent clauses, “however” is preceded by a semicolon and followed by a comma.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses the possessive apostrophe correctly for a plural noun?
o: The farmers union’s met the minister.
The farmers’ union met the minister.
The farmer’s union represents all farmers in the province.
The farmers’s union met the minister.
explanation: For a union of many farmers the possessive is “farmers’”; the others place the apostrophe wrongly or add an extra s.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses a colon to introduce a list correctly?
o: Bring the following documents: your CNIC, two photographs and your degree.
Please bring: your CNIC, two photographs and your degree.
The documents are: your CNIC, two photographs and your degree.
Bring your: CNIC, two photographs and degree.
explanation: A colon introducing a list must follow a complete clause such as “Bring the following documents”.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is punctuated correctly as a question?
o: She asked where the post office was?
Where the post office is I do not know?
Could you tell me where the post office is?
I wonder where the post office is?
explanation: Only the first is a direct question (a polite request); the others are statements containing indirect questions and end with full stops.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses commas correctly around a non-defining clause?
o: My uncle, who teaches, history lives in Hyderabad.
Our principal who retired last year, still visits the school.
My aunt, who is a doctor works in Quetta.
My elder brother, who lives in Dubai, is visiting us.
explanation: A non-defining clause is enclosed by a pair of commas, one before and one after it; the others omit one comma or misplace it.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses “its” or “it’s” correctly?
o: It’s time the city repaired it’s roads.
Its time the city repaired its roads.
It’s time the city repaired its roads.
Its time the city repaired it’s roads.
explanation: “It’s” is short for “it is”, and “its” is the possessive; the first sentence uses each correctly.

subject: English
q: Which sentence correctly punctuates an introductory clause?
o: Because, the road was closed we took a detour.
When the bell rang, the students left the room.
If it rains the match, will be postponed.
Although he was tired; he kept working.
explanation: A comma separates the introductory clause from the main clause; the others misplace the comma or use a semicolon after a dependent clause.

subject: English
q: Which sentence contains an unnecessary comma?
o: The man who repaired our roof, lives next door.
Yes, the roof has been repaired.
After the storm, the roof was repaired.
Our neighbour, a retired teacher, repaired our roof.
explanation: In the first sentence the comma separates the subject (with its defining clause) from the verb “lives”, which is incorrect.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses the semicolon incorrectly?
o: Although he was tired; he finished the essay.
He visited Lahore, Pakistan; Delhi, India; and Dhaka, Bangladesh.
He was tired; he still finished the essay.
He was tired; nevertheless, he finished the essay.
explanation: A semicolon cannot join a dependent clause (“Although he was tired”) to a main clause; a comma is needed.

subject: English
q: Which of these sentences has a misplaced apostrophe?
o: The book’s are on the shelf.
explanation: A simple plural such as “books” takes no apostrophe.

subject: English
q: Which sentence correctly punctuates the date?
o: The school was founded on June, 5 1950 by a local trader.
Pakistan came into being on August 14, 1947, after years of struggle.
The library was inaugurated on, May 9 1990 by the mayor.
The new bridge was opened on March 3 2021, after, years of work.
explanation: In the month–day–year style, a comma separates the day from the year and another follows the year in mid-sentence; the others misplace the commas.

subject: English
q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly with a name in direct address?
o: Please wait here, for a moment sir.
Thank you for your help, Doctor.
Come, in Ahmed and take a seat.
explanation: A name or title in direct address is set off by a comma; the others place the comma wrongly or leave the name unmarked.

subject: English
q: Choose the punctuation mark that correctly fills the gap: “The guard wouldn___t let us in without passes”
explanation: The contraction of “would not” is “wouldn’t”, with an apostrophe for the missing letter.

subject: English
q: Which punctuation mark should fill the blank in: “Faiz Ahmad Faiz was a well___known poet of the subcontinent”?
explanation: A compound adjective placed before a noun (“well-known poet”) is hyphenated.

subject: English
q: Choose the punctuation mark that correctly fills the gap: “After a close contest, the mayor was re___elected for a second term”
explanation: The prefix “re-” is hyphenated before a word beginning with “e” to avoid the double vowel: “re-elected”.

subject: English
q: Which punctuation mark should fill the blank in: “The flight was cancelled for a simple reason ___ the runway was flooded”?
explanation: A colon introduces an explanation of what has just been announced (“a simple reason”).

subject: English
q: Choose the punctuation mark that correctly fills the gap: “The shops were closed for Eid ___ so we bought our groceries a day earlier”
explanation: A comma precedes “so” when it joins two independent clauses.

subject: English
q: Which punctuation mark should fill the blank in: “Peshawar ___ one of the oldest cities in South Asia, is the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa”?
explanation: The appositive “one of the oldest cities in South Asia” is enclosed by a pair of commas; the closing comma is already in place.

subject: English
q: Choose the punctuation mark that correctly fills the gap: “Yes ___ the application has been received”
explanation: An introductory “yes” or “no” is followed by a comma.

subject: English
q: Which punctuation mark should fill the blank in: “Submit the form before Friday ___ otherwise, your application will be rejected”?
explanation: “Otherwise” here is a conjunctive adverb linking two independent clauses, so it is preceded by a semicolon.

subject: English
q: Choose the punctuation mark that correctly fills the gap: “The transporters went on strike ___ consequently, prices of vegetables doubled overnight”
explanation: A semicolon comes before the conjunctive adverb “consequently” when it joins two independent clauses.

subject: English
q: Which punctuation mark should fill the blank in: “You have submitted the fee, haven’t you ___”?
explanation: A sentence ending in a question tag (“haven’t you”) takes a question mark.

subject: English
q: Choose the punctuation mark that correctly fills the gap: “I would like to know whether the post is still vacant ___”
explanation: This is a statement containing an indirect question, so it ends with a full stop.

subject: English
q: Where should a comma be placed in: “Tired after the long journey the pilgrims rested at the inn.”?
explanation: An introductory participial phrase is followed by a comma, which here comes after “journey”.

subject: English
q: Where should a comma be placed in: “Please sign here sir.”?
explanation: A term of direct address at the end of a sentence is preceded by a comma: “Please sign here, sir.”

subject: English
q: Where does the missing comma belong in: “I will be late” she said.
o: After “late”, inside the closing quotation mark
explanation: When direct speech comes before the reporting clause, a comma ends the quoted words inside the quotation marks.

subject: English
q: Which word needs an apostrophe? “Whos going to chair the meeting on Monday?”
explanation: “Who’s” is the contraction of “who is”, so it needs an apostrophe.

subject: English
q: Which word needs an apostrophe? “The ministers speech was broadcast live on every channel.” (One minister is meant.)
explanation: The possessive of the singular “minister” is “minister’s”.

subject: English
q: Which word needs an apostrophe? “Candidates shouldnt bring mobile phones into the hall.”
explanation: The contraction of “should not” is “shouldn’t”.

subject: English
q: Which expression needs hyphens? “The hospital has installed state of the art equipment in its newly built wing.”
explanation: A phrase used as a compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated: “state-of-the-art equipment”; “newly built” contains an -ly adverb.

subject: English
q: Which expression needs a hyphen? “She obtained a first class degree from the university in the capital.”
explanation: A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated: “a first-class degree”.

subject: English
q: Which expression needs a hyphen? “Women must have a greater role in decision making at the local level.”
explanation: “Decision-making” is a compound noun formed from a noun and a gerund and is conventionally hyphenated.

subject: English
q: In the sentence The teacher said, “Open your books” — where should the full stop go?
explanation: When a quoted sentence ends the whole sentence, the full stop goes inside the closing quotation mark.

subject: English
q: Why is there a comma after “However” in: “However, the proposal was rejected.”?
o: It separates an introductory conjunctive adverb from the clause
explanation: A conjunctive adverb at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma.
